Simple N-gram Idea and Its Limitations in LLMs What is an N-gram? An N-gram is a sequence of N consecutive words (or tokens) in a sentence. N-gram language models predict the next word using only the previous (N−1) words.

Definition: An N-gram language model estimates the probability of the next word based on the last N−1 words in the sequence. They are the foundation for statistical text generation, speech recognition, and autocomplete.

BERT solves these problems by understanding context from both directions simultaneously. Example of Bidirectional Understanding Consider the sentence: The bank is near the river. Here, bank means the side of a river. Now consider: She deposited money in the bank.

Transformer model: A Transformer model is a deep learning architecture introduced in the 2017 paper "Attention Is All You Need." It revolutionized artificial intelligence by replacing recurrent processing (used in RNNs and LSTMs) with an attention mechanism, allowing models to process all input tokens in parallel. This made training faster and enabled models to capture

Transformer is a neural network architecture used for various machine learning tasks, especially in natural language processing and computer vision. It focuses on understanding relationships within data to process information more effectively.  Uses attention mechanisms to capture relationships between inputs  Processes entire sequences at once instead of step by step  Improves performance on tasks involving context and dependencies  Widely used across NLP, vision and other AI applications Key Components of a Transformer 1. GPT (Generative Pre-trained Transformer) Model The GPT (Generative Pre-trained Transformer) model is a family of Large Language Models (LLMs) developed by OpenAI. It is based on the Transformer architecture and is designed to understand and generate human-like text.  G – Generative: Generates new text based on the given input.  P – Pre-trained: Learns language patterns from a very large collection of text before being used for specific tasks.  T – Transformer: Uses the Transformer architecture with a self-attention mechanism. Definition GPT is a decoder-only Transformer model that predicts the next word (token) in a
sequence to generate coherent and context-aware text. GPT Architecture GPT uses only the decoder part of the Transformer. Input Prompt │ Tokenization │ Word Embeddings │ Positional Encoding │
│ Transformer Decoder Block 1│ │ Transformer Decoder Block 2│ │ Transformer Decoder Block N│ │ Linear Layer │ Softmax │ Next Token Prediction │ Generated Text Main Components of GPT

1. Input Tokenization  The input sentence is divided into tokens (words or subwords). Example: Input: "Artificial Intelligence is amazing." Tokens: ["Artificial", "Intelligence", "is", "amazing", "."] 2. Embedding Layer Each token is converted into a numerical vector called an embedding. Example: Token Embedding Artificial [0.21, -0.56, ...] Intelligence [0.48, 0.17, ...] 3. Positional Encoding Since GPT processes all tokens simultaneously during training, positional information is added. Example: Artificial → Position 1 Intelligence → Position 2 is → Position 3 amazing → Position 4 4. Masked Self-Attention

GPT uses masked (causal) self-attention, which means it can only look at the current and previous tokens—not future ones. Example: Sentence: I love learning AI When predicting "AI", GPT can attend to: I love learning It cannot look at "AI" before predicting it. This allows GPT to generate text one token at a time. 5. Feed-Forward Neural Network Each decoder layer contains a feed-forward network that further processes the attention output. 6. Linear Layer + Softmax The model computes the probability of every possible next token.

Example: Input: "The capital of India is" Output Probabilities: Delhi → 96% Mumbai → 2% Chennai → 1% Kolkata → 1% GPT selects the next token according to the decoding strategy (greedy, temperature, top-k, top-p, etc.). How GPT Works Step 1: Pre-training GPT is trained on massive text datasets using next-token prediction. Example: Input: "The sun rises in the" Target: "east" After seeing billions of examples, GPT learns:  grammar  vocabulary  reasoning patterns  facts present in its training data  language structure Step 2: Fine-tuning / Instruction Tuning The pre-trained model is further adapted to follow instructions and produce more helpful,

safer, and conversational responses. Step 3: Text Generation When a user enters a prompt, GPT predicts one token at a time until the response is complete. Example: Prompt: "What is Machine Learning?" ↓ Predicts: Machine-->Learning-->is-->a-->branch-->of-->Artificial-->Intelligence. Features of GPT  Generates human-like text  Understands context from previous tokens  Supports long conversations  Answers questions  Summarizes documents

 Translates languages  Writes code  Creates stories, emails, and reports Applications of GPT  AI chatbots  Virtual assistants  Content generation  Text summarization  Language translation  Code generation and debugging  Question answering  Email drafting  Report writing  Educational tutoring Advantages  Produces fluent, coherent text.  Handles many language tasks without task-specific programming.  Learns from large-scale pre-training.  Can generate creative and context-aware responses.  Scales effectively to larger models and datasets. Limitations  Can generate incorrect or fabricated information (hallucinations).

 Quality depends on the prompt and available context.  May reflect biases present in training data.  Requires significant computational resources for training.  Does not inherently verify facts or perform real-time reasoning about new events unless connected to external tools or up-to-date data. Summary on Open-Source LLMs Definition Open-source Large Language Models (LLMs) are AI models whose model architecture, source code, and often the model weights are publicly available. This allows researchers, developers, and organizations to use, modify, fine-tune, and deploy them for various

applications without building a model from scratch. Unlike closed-source models, open-source LLMs provide greater transparency, customization, and flexibility. Key Characteristics  Publicly available for research and development.  Can be fine-tuned for specific tasks.  Support local deployment on private servers or personal computers (depending on model size).  Encourage collaboration and innovation through community contributions.  Often available under open or permissive licenses (license terms vary by model). Introduction to Prompts in LLMs A prompt is the instruction, question, or input given to a Large Language Model (LLM) to guide it in generating a response. In simple words: Prompt = What you tell the AI to do For example, if you ask ChatGPT: “Explain machine learning in simple words.” This sentence is a prompt, and the explanation generated by the LLM is the response/output. 1. Importance of Prompts (or) Role of Prompts in Interacting with LLMs [Page 54 Visuals: Contains 2 embedded image/diagram object(s) — call inspect_source_image with page=54 if visual details are required]

Prompts act as a communication interface between the user and the LLM. They provide the model with information about the user's requirement. LLMs can perform many tasks, but the quality of the output depends greatly on how clearly the task is described. A well-designed prompt helps the model understand: A prompt can tell the LLM:  What to do – explain, summarize, translate, generate, classify, etc.  What information should be used  Who the answer is for  What format the output should have  How much detail to provide  What limitations or constraints should be followed 2. Basic structure of a prompt

A prompt may contain several components: Instruction + Context + Examples + Constraints + Output Format For example: Instruction: Explain photosynthesis. Context: The explanation is for a 10th-grade student. Constraint: Use simple language. Output format: Give 5 bullet points. The LLM can then generate an answer appropriate for that requirement. 3. Simple examples Prompt Expected Output “What is AI?” Definition of AI “Translate ‘Good morning’ into Hindi.” Hindi translation “Summarize this paragraph in 3 sentences.” Short summary “Write Python code to add two numbers.” Python program “Explain TCP/IP using a simple example.” Easy explanation with example

4. Poor prompt vs. good prompt Poor prompt: Tell me about AI. This is very broad. Better prompt: Explain Artificial Intelligence to a beginner in simple language. Give its definition, three applications, and one real-world example. The second prompt provides clear instructions and constraints, so the expected output is more focused. 5. Prompt engineering Prompt engineering is the practice of designing and refining prompts to obtain useful, accurate, and consistent responses from an LLM. Common prompt-design techniques include:  Clear instructions

 Providing context  Giving examples  Specifying constraints  Specifying the desired output format  Assigning a role when useful  Breaking complex tasks into smaller steps 6. Example of a well-designed prompt Role: You are a computer science teacher. Task: Explain the Transformer model. Audience: Undergraduate students. Requirement: Explain the main components and give a simple example. Format: Use headings and bullet points. This gives the LLM much more guidance than simply saying: “Explain Transformer.” Note: Prompting is the process of giving instructions or inputs to an LLM so that it produces the

desired output. Effective prompts are usually clear, specific, contextual, and well-structured. Basic idea: User Prompt → LLM processes the prompt → Generated Response Responsible Prompting Responsible prompting means designing and using prompts in a safe, ethical, fair, and careful way so that the LLM produces useful outputs without causing harm, spreading misinformation, violating privacy, or encouraging inappropriate behavior. In simple words: Responsible prompting = Asking AI to perform a task in a safe, ethical, and trustworthy manner. 1. Why is responsible prompting important? LLMs can generate incorrect, biased, sensitive, or harmful content. A responsible prompt

helps reduce these risks and encourages the model to provide appropriate answers. For example: Less responsible prompt: “Give me personal information about this person.” Responsible prompt: “Provide publicly available professional information about this person, and avoid private or sensitive personal details.” 2. Key principles of responsible prompting Principle Meaning Example Clarity Give clear and specific instructions “Explain TCP/IP in 5 simple points.”

Accuracy Ask the model to avoid unsupported claims “If you are uncertain, clearly state the uncertainty.” Privacy Do not request or expose sensitive personal information Avoid passwords, medical records, etc. Fairness Avoid discriminatory or biased instructions “Compare candidates using job- related qualifications.” Safety Avoid instructions that could cause harm Ask for safe and legal alternatives. Transparency Make AI-generated content identifiable when appropriate State that content was AI-assisted. Verification Check important information independently Verify facts using reliable sources.

Respect Avoid hateful, abusive, or degrading instructions Use neutral and respectful language. 3. Responsible prompting example Suppose you want an LLM to generate information about a medical topic. Poor prompt: “Tell me exactly what disease this person has based on these symptoms.” More responsible prompt: “Explain possible causes of these symptoms in general terms. Do not make a definitive diagnosis. Mention when professional medical evaluation may be appropriate.” The second prompt recognizes that an LLM should not be treated as a substitute for professional diagnosis. 4. Responsible prompting and privacy

Users should avoid putting unnecessary sensitive information into prompts. For example, instead of: “Analyze this patient record containing their name, phone number, address, and medical history.” Use: “Analyze this anonymized patient case. Remove names, contact details, and other identifying information.” 5. Responsible prompting for education A student can use AI responsibly by asking for explanations and guidance rather than simply requesting work to submit as their own. For example: “Explain the concept of deadlock in operating systems and give me practice questions so I can solve them myself.”
This promotes learning rather than blind copying. 6. A useful responsible prompt pattern A simple structure is: Task + Context + Constraints + Safety/Accuracy requirement + Output format

Example: “Explain Generative AI to undergraduate students using simple language. Give three real-world examples. Avoid unsupported claims and clearly mention any limitations. Present the answer using headings and bullet points.” 7. Responsible prompting does not guarantee correct answers An important point is: A responsible prompt can reduce risks, but it cannot guarantee that an LLM's response is always correct or unbiased. Therefore, users should review, verify, and critically evaluate important AI-generated information. Note: Responsible prompting is the practice of designing prompts that guide an AI system to generate safe,
ethical, accurate, fair, privacy-preserving, and appropriate responses while considering the limitations and potential risks of AI.
